extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers and performers interested in the theory and practice of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating and analysing comedy across media (theatre, film, stand-up, television, radio, prose). Covers historical definitions, theories of humour, genres, techniques, and form-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genre of dramatic works intended to be humorous or amusing by inducing laughter, especially in theatre, film, stand-up comedy, television, radio, books, or any other entertainment medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the range of media and the primary goal (inducing laughter); useful as a high-level criterion for whether a work belongs to the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian ridiculing / imitation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle defined comedy as an imitation of men worse than the average: the Ridiculous may be defined as a mistake or deformity not productive of pain or harm to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters and situations that reveal ridiculousness (mistakes/deformities) without causing real harm; historically rooted standard for comic characterization and ethical boundary of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle: comic narrative pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedies begin with low or base characters seeking insignificant aims and end with some accomplishment of the aims which either lightens the initial baseness or reveals the insignificance of the aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure stories so that protagonists start from humble or trivial aims and end in a resolution that reframes or redeems the initial condition (often a happy/positive ending in classical usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity / contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologists agree the predominant characteristics are incongruity or contrast in the object (mismatch between expectation and reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create humor by setting up expectations and subverting them with surprising, contrasting, or illogical outcomes; central to many comic devices (parody, non-sequiturs, surreal humour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shock / emotional seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: Shock or emotional seizure on the part of the subject is a predominant characteristic connected with laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise or sudden emotional jolts can provoke laughter; used deliberately in dark or coarse comedy but can risk offense if mishandled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of superiority is an essential factor: Thomas Hobbes speaks of laughter as a 'sudden glory'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor often arises when the audience feels superior to a character's mistake or folly; use with care to avoid mean-spiritedness or harm to real individuals/groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic frame (rhetorical stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kenneth Burke's 'comic frame' is 'neither wholly euphemistic, nor wholly debunking'—it provides a charitable attitude required for persuasion while maintaining shrewdness; it satirizes to promote change without vilification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a tone that mocks folly while preserving empathy; examples include satirical news shows that mix crude humor with serious critique (e.g., The Daily Show).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire / political satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire and political satire use comedy to portray people or social institutions as ridiculous or corrupt, thus alienating their audience from the object of their humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exaggeration, irony, and ridicule aimed at institutions or attitudes to provoke critical distance and potential change; be aware of ethical and factual responsibilities when targeting real subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody subverts popular genres and forms, critiquing those forms without necessarily condemning them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate conventions of a genre closely enough to be recognizable, then twist or exaggerate them to expose weaknesses or absurdities; effective parody requires knowledge of the source conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of social conventions / taboo humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Scatological humour, sexual humour, and race humour create comedy by violating social conventions or taboos in comic ways, which can often be taken as offensive by the subjects of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such humor trades on transgression; creators must weigh comedic payoff against potential harm or alienation of audiences and targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surreal / absurdist humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Surreal humour is predicated on deliberate violations of causal reasoning, producing events and behaviours that are obviously illogical (bizarre juxtapositions, non-sequiturs, irrational situations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on unpredictability and illogic to subvert expectations; examples include Lewis Carroll and Edward Lear; roots in avant-garde movements like Dada and Surrealism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique in which comedians focus on their misfortunes and foibles to entertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using oneself as the butt of jokes can create rapport and defuse hostility; common in stand-up and personal storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screwball comedy technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Derives its humor largely from bizarre, surprising (and improbable) situations or characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct rapid-fire, improbable interactions and situations; often used in romantic or fast-paced film comedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black (dark) comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterized by a form of humor that includes darker aspects of human behavior or human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine grim or taboo subjects for irony and dark amusement; requires careful tonal control to avoid gratuitousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically takes as its subject a particular part of society (usually upper-class society) and uses humor to parody or satirize the behavior and mannerisms of its members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and exaggerate social conventions, affectations, and hypocrisies of a social class to create comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic comedy conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicts burgeoning romance in humorous terms and focuses on the foibles of those who are falling in love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance romantic stakes with comic obstacles and character flaws; often resolves in reconciliation or union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-up comedy mode
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of comic performance in which the performer addresses the audience directly, usually speaking in their own person rather than as a dramatic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise direct address, persona, timing, and audience interaction; craft punchlines and callbacks suited to live performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Xiangsheng (crosstalk) techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Xiangsheng is usually a rapid dialogue between two people which emphasizes word play and allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quick repartee, puns, and cultural allusions; success depends on linguistic dexterity and shared references with the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rakugo storytelling technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Rakugo is a form of comic storytelling in which a single seated performer narrates humorous tales using dialogue, vocal variation, and minimal props.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on voice, timing, and minimal physicality to distinguish characters and sustain a long-form comic tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commedia dell'arte / stock-character improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: A tradition using stock characters and improvised performance (e.g., Pulcinella / Punch), often anarchic and subversive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop recognizable archetypal characters and rely on improvisation within established scenarios; physicality and masks/props are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespearean / Elizabethan comedy convention
rubrics_metrics.description: In Elizabethan usage, a comedy is one that has a happy ending, usually involving marriages between the unmarried characters, and a tone more light-hearted than other plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works evoking this tradition, incorporate reconciliations, marriages, or restorations of social harmony as part of comic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coarse language as a framing device
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing coarse language into an otherwise serious commentary can serve to frame the segment comically, creating a serious tone underlying the comedic agenda (example: The Daily Show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coarse language can produce contrast and release; employ it strategically to underline critique while being mindful of audience expectations and broadcast standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic timing and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic timing (listed among topics) is a central practical element of successful comedy performance and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pacing, pause, emphasis, and rhythm are essential to landing jokes and shaping audience response; tailor timing to medium (stage, screen, radio, text).
